source: Hart (1965) Memory and the feeling-of-knowing experience
finding: Founding FOK study. People fail to recall an item, rate whether they would recognise it, then take a recognition test. FOK predicted later recognition above chance, so the feeling carries real information about what is stored.
numbers: No numbers available. Read only through a secondary summary, not the 1965 paper.
quote: Examined the accuracy of feeling-of-knowing judgments
limits: Procedure details are from general knowledge, not verified. Open the paper in a later pass.
agent_relevance: Hart's logic maps to S0: a cheap pre-attempt rating can predict success without solving the task.

source: Nelson & Narens (1990) Metamemory: a theoretical framework and new findings
finding: Two-level model. Object level holds cognition. Meta level holds a model of it. Monitoring is flow up (ease-of-learning, JOL, FOK, confidence). Control is flow down (allocate study time, pick search strategy, stop search). Applies at acquisition, retention and retrieval.
numbers: Qualitative framework; no numbers.
quote: Monitoring and control occur during acquisition, retention, and retrieval.
limits: Read through a secondary summary, not the chapter. Gives vocabulary, not quantitative predictions.
agent_relevance: Template for the schema: monitor signals feed control operators. An S0 'will this be easy' gate is an ease-of-learning monitor feeding a control choice.

source: Reder & Ritter (1992) What determines initial feeling of knowing? Familiarity with question terms, not with the answer
finding: Cue-familiarity account. People can judge whether they know an answer before trying to retrieve it, because they react to familiarity of the question terms, not to the stored answer.
numbers: No numbers read.
quote: Judgments depend on the question (cue), not the actual memory (target)
limits: Secondary summary only. Koriat and Levy (2001) say familiarity acts first and accessibility is added when familiarity is not enough.
agent_relevance: A prompt full of familiar terms may inflate an 'I know this' signal. S0 should not rely on surface familiarity alone.

source: Koriat (1993) accessibility account of FOK; Koriat & Levy (2001) interactive hypothesis
finding: Accessibility account: FOK comes from how much partial information comes to mind, right or wrong. Interactive hypothesis: cue familiarity is used first and quickly; accessibility is added when familiarity is not enough.
numbers: No effect sizes read.
limits: Secondary summary only. Partial information can be wrong, so FOK is accurate only when what comes to mind is mostly right.
agent_relevance: Suggests a two-step S0: fast familiarity check, then a probe of what partial content the model can actually produce.

source: Koriat (2026) Confidence judgments, feelings of knowing and judgments of learning: towards a common framework (Memory & Cognition)
finding: Extends the Self-Consistency Model of confidence to FOK and JOL. Judgment comes from consistency among cues sampled from a shared pool. Both FOK and JOL show a consensuality effect (stronger judgment when more people make the same choice) and a replicability effect.
numbers: Study 3, 100 children grades 1-6, 24 paired associates. Consensual JOL strength M=73.22 vs nonconsensual M=60.87, t(71)=8.24, p<.0001. Majority size averaged 74.3%. Between-child correlation of JOL with others' choices averaged .44; within-item .32. Related pairs 71.8 vs 58.1; unrelated pairs 64.3 vs 62.5.
quote: confidence in their choice is based on the consistency with which the selected option is supported across the retrieved cues
limits: One research group's model. JOL part uses children and paired associates. Effect shrinks for unrelated pairs.
agent_relevance: A judgment is partly a vote among sampled cues. Sampling several independent self-checks and measuring agreement is a model-based way to get a confidence signal.

source: Koriat (1975/1976) phonetic symbolism guessing and confidence, as reported in Koriat (2026)
finding: People guessed word meanings across languages they did not know and still gave confidence ratings that tracked accuracy. This puzzle started the cue-consistency line of work.
numbers: Correct matching rose from 53% at rating 1 to 66% at rating 4 on a 4-point scale. Matching was above chance.
limits: Reported second-hand inside the 2026 paper; original not opened. Task was retrospective confidence, though the title said feeling of knowing.
agent_relevance: Monitoring can work without access to the answer, from cue patterns. A model's signal can be informative even where it cannot solve the task.

source: Tekin & Roediger (2021) The effect of delayed judgments of learning on retention (Metacognition and Learning)
finding: Delayed JOLs predict memory better than immediate JOLs (Nelson & Dunlosky 1991). Three experiments asked whether making delayed JOLs also changes memory. Cue-only delayed JOLs gave poorer later recall than overt retrieval in Exp 2a and 2b. In Exp 1 they did not differ reliably from restudy or retrieval.
numbers: Final cued recall delayed by two days. 12% of 2400 overt-retrieval trials timed out at 8 s. Quotes Rhodes & Tauber (2011): 98 effect sizes, delayed JOL benefit g=0.08 overall; g=0.70 for cue-target delayed JOLs, g=0.03 for cue-only.
quote: only some delayed JOLs elicit covert retrieval attempts
limits: Supports a truncated-search idea. Rhodes & Tauber numbers are quoted, not read in the original.
agent_relevance: Delayed, cue-only ratings are more diagnostic. For an agent: rate difficulty after a short probe attempt, not while the problem text is fresh and visible.

source: Rhodes & Tauber (2011) The influence of delaying judgments of learning on metacognitive accuracy: a meta-analytic review, as cited in Tekin & Roediger (2021)
finding: Meta-analysis of the delayed-JOL effect. Only its retention comparison is recorded here.
numbers: 98 effect sizes; g=0.08 overall; cue-target g=0.70; cue-only g=0.03 (retention outcome, as quoted).
limits: Original not opened. The accuracy effect size itself is not recorded. Open it in a later pass.
agent_relevance: Flag: fetch the accuracy difference (delayed vs immediate gamma).

source: Hughes & Thomas (2022) When memory and metamemory align: how processes at encoding influence delayed JOL accuracy (J. Intelligence)
finding: Delayed JOLs are accurate because they use cues from long-term memory. Study technique changes this: when a technique makes the target easier to retrieve at JOL time, delayed-JOL accuracy rises. Techniques: reading twice, keyword generation, test with feedback.
numbers: Two experiments; 3x2 mixed design (technique x related vs unrelated pairs). 38 of 99 participants had a missing gamma for one item type. Target accessibility positively associated with delayed-JOL accuracy.
quote: the accessibility of targets was positively associated with delayed-JOL accuracy
limits: Gamma has missing-value problems in small cells. Exact gamma means not recorded.
agent_relevance: Monitoring accuracy depends on what earlier processing left behind. If the attempt leaves retrievable traces (worked steps), later self-rating is better.

source: Tian et al. (2021) Beliefs about font size and the font size effect on JOLs: is word frequency a moderator? (PLoS ONE)
finding: Large fonts raise JOLs without helping memory. Beliefs about font size drive this for low-frequency words but not high-frequency words. A meta-analysis supported moderation by word frequency.
numbers: Exp 1: 70 pt vs 9 pt x high vs low frequency, within subjects. Beliefs did not mediate when both cues were present. Exp 2: belief contribution present in a pure list of low-frequency words, absent in a pure list of high-frequency words.
limits: Exact effect sizes not recorded. Boundary condition: cue effects depend on what other cues are present.
agent_relevance: Judgments follow surface cues (illusions of competence). A difficulty gate that reads only form (prompt length, wording) can be fooled the same way.

source: Undorf & Broder (2021) Metamemory for pictures of naturalistic scenes: accuracy and cue utilization (Memory & Cognition)
finding: Three experiments. JOLs for scene pictures were substantially accurate. People combine several cues. Intrinsic cues (peacefulness, people present) and extrinsic cues (presentation frequency, semantic distinctiveness) mostly predicted real recognition.
numbers: Relative accuracy scored with gamma and with Brunswik's matching index G, because gamma mixes competence with noise and has inflated type 1 error (cites Broder & Undorf 2019; Murayama 2014).
limits: Exact gamma and G values not recorded. Pictures, not words.
agent_relevance: Use accuracy measures that do not conflate skill with noise when scoring any difficulty gate.

source: Yamato & Suzuki (2022) Evolution of metamemory based on self-reference to own memory in neural networks with neuromodulation (Sci. Reports)
finding: Evolved small neural networks with neuromodulation show a metamemory function by referring to their own memory state. The evolved structure resembles the Nelson-Narens model.
numbers: Abstract and introduction only; no benchmark numbers.
limits: Toy networks, not language models. Results not read in depth.
agent_relevance: A monitor that reads the memory state, not the answer, is enough to build a Nelson-Narens loop.

source: Tip-of-the-tongue and feeling-of-knowing effects on metacognitive sensitivity of recognition confidence (general recognition theory study, 2025)
finding: Used a multidimensional signal detection model. After a recall failure, a tip-of-the-tongue state or a high FOK was linked to higher metacognitive sensitivity of later recognition confidence.
numbers: Two experiments: famous names (Exp 1) and general-knowledge questions (Exp 2). Two GRT models fitted; sensitivity curves built against TOT or FOK strength.
quote: experiencing a TOT or a high FOK is associated with an increase in metacognitive sensitivity of confidence judgments
limits: Authors and venue not captured in the page text I read; citation approximate. Effect sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: After a retrieval failure, a strong partial-access signal makes later confidence more trustworthy. Keep a failed-attempt probe in S0.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false items. They can judge P(True) of their own samples. They can also be trained to predict P(IK), the chance they know the answer before answering. P(IK) transfers partly to new tasks but calibration breaks out of distribution.
numbers: Models 800M, 3B, 12B, 52B. Ground-truth P(IK) from 30 samples per TriviaQA question at T=1, 10-shot prompt. IK label if ground-truth P(IK)>0.5. At 52B, answers with P(True)>0.5 are far more often correct than generic ones. Obscure question 'What state's rodeo hall of fame was established in 2013?' gets P(IK)=18%. GSM8k AUROC roughly 0.69 (TriviaQA-only training) vs 0.75 (trained on four tasks); the table layout was ambiguous in my text extraction.
quote: models trained on TriviaQA have significant power to differentiate between math, lambada, and code questions that they can answer
limits: Needs a finetuned value head; zero-shot P(IK) is poor. RLHF policies are miscalibrated unless temperature-tuned. Models are biased against 'none of the above'. Models are only somewhat better at predicting their own P(IK) than another model's, so P(IK) may partly track task difficulty.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of a pre-attempt FOK. Supports an S0 gate, but a learned or calibrated gate is needed; a bare prompt is weak.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) P(IK) responds to source text and hints
finding: P(IK) rises when helpful context is added. On GSM8k it rises more for correct hints than for distracting hints, and more of a hint gives higher P(IK). This looks like accessibility-style monitoring.
numbers: 52B model. Wikipedia article on the rodeo question lifts P(IK) above 18%. GSM8k good hints give higher P(IK) than bad model-generated hints; the model trained on four tasks is more consistent with partial hints.
quote: P(IK) appropriately predicts a low value, specifically 18% for a 52B model
limits: Seen in a trained value head, not a prompt.
agent_relevance: Re-run the S0 gate after retrieval or hints are added, since access changes the estimate.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) self-evaluation improves with many samples
finding: Showing the model many of its own T=1 samples to the same question improves its judgement of any one sample. This resembles self-consistency but is done by the model.
numbers: k-shot comparison examples help mostly by improving calibration, not AUROC. Self-evaluation improves with size in almost all cases at 52B.
quote: showing the model many T = 1 samples for a single question significantly improves its ability to evaluate
limits: Costs several samples per question.
agent_relevance: Samples as evidence: a cheap proxy for a retrieval-ease signal.

source: Lin, Hilton & Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 finetuned on arithmetic examples (CalibratedMath, 21 tasks) outputs a number or word for confidence that is calibrated, also under distribution shift. The result is not explained by logits or by simple heuristics such as integer size.
numbers: Training set: Add-subtract; about 100 questions per sub-task, about 10k inputs; label is GPT-3's empirical accuracy on the sub-task (100 x p). Words setup uses five bins of width 0.2. Eval sets: Multi-answer and Multiply-divide. Constant baseline on Multi-answer MSE 37.4 / MAD 33.7 in my extraction; verbalized finetuned scores beat baselines but table columns were garbled, so exact per-row values are not claimed.
limits: Calibration is against sub-task accuracy, so it may track task type, not item difficulty. Smaller models (GPT-J, 7B GPT-3) too weak to test.
agent_relevance: An LLM can emit an ease-style rating trained on its own accuracy per task class. Direct template for a class-level S0 estimate.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration: eliciting calibrated confidence from RLHF language models
finding: For RLHF chat models, asking for a verbalized probability gives better calibration than reading token probabilities. Asking for top-k guesses first helps more.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo TriviaQA: label-prob ECE 0.140, AUC 0.869; verbalized 1-stage top-2 ECE 0.050, AUC 0.894. SciQ: label-prob ECE 0.256 vs verbalized top-4 ECE 0.065 (AUC 0.752 vs 0.763). TruthfulQA: ECE 0.451 vs top-4 0.203, but AUC 0.418 vs 0.455. GPT-4 TriviaQA: label-prob ECE 0.078, verbalized 1S top-1 ECE 0.024. Abstract: often cuts ECE by a relative 50%.
quote: verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: Calibration (ECE) improves much more than discrimination (AUC). On TruthfulQA AUC is below 0.5 for several methods.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only gate is cheap and gives a usable prior, but it may not separate hard from easy items. Do not let it decide alone.

source: Yin et al. (2023) Do large language models know what they don't know?
finding: SelfAware dataset: 1,032 unanswerable questions in five categories plus 2,337 answerable ones. 20 LLMs tested at spotting unanswerable questions. Bigger models do better. In-context examples and instruction tuning help. GPT-4 is best but below humans.
numbers: GPT-4 F1 75.47%. Human F1 84.93%. Instruction tuning and examples narrow the gap between davinci and text-davinci.
limits: Tests knowing that a question is unanswerable, not item-level memory strength. Human baseline from a small annotator group.
agent_relevance: Direct measure of refusal-worthiness. An S0 gate for 'unanswerable' lagged humans by about 9 F1 points for the best model then.

source: Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty: linguistic invariances for uncertainty estimation in natural language generation
finding: Semantic entropy groups sampled answers by meaning before computing entropy. It predicts answer correctness better than sequence-likelihood entropy, lexical similarity and p(True) on TriviaQA and CoQA, and improves with model size.
numbers: AUROC near 0.78 on TriviaQA for the largest model in Fig 1a (from text extraction; verify against the figure). Also studies number of distinct answers and a temperature trade-off between accuracy and diversity.
quote: semantic entropy has a significantly higher AUROC than entropy in sequence-probability-space
limits: Needs several samples per question. Gain varies by dataset and model size.
agent_relevance: A sample-agreement signal, close to Koriat's self-consistency idea: sample several times and check whether the meanings agree.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? An empirical evaluation of confidence elicitation in LLMs
finding: Black-box study of verbalized confidence, sampling and aggregation. LLMs verbalize overconfidently, possibly imitating human speech. Human-inspired prompts and agreement across samples reduce this. White-box methods are only somewhat better. No method wins everywhere, and hard professional-knowledge tasks stay poor.
numbers: Five LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat, eight tasks. GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna average ECE above 0.377. GPT-4 vanilla verbalized average AUROC only 62.7%. White-box vs black-box AUROC 0.522 to 0.605 in the abstract.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns
limits: Large variation across datasets. Professional-knowledge tasks weakest.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a single verbalized number for S0. Combine it with sample agreement.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know (Nature Machine Intelligence)
finding: People reading default LLM explanations overrate the LLM's accuracy and cannot tell right from wrong answers: a calibration gap and a discrimination gap. Matching explanation length and wording to the model's real confidence narrows both gaps.
numbers: Model confidence AUC .751 (GPT-3.5) and .746 (PaLM2) on multiple choice, .781 (GPT-4o) short answer. Human AUC on default explanations .589, .602, .592. Mean participant AUC .54 and .57 for long and short explanations in Exp 2a-2c. LLM overconfident on multiple choice, somewhat underconfident on short answer. 350 questions; GPT-3.5 55% and PaLM2 50% accurate.
limits: Reader side, not LLM self-monitoring. The gaps narrow but remain.
agent_relevance: Wording shapes how confidence is read. The agent should state confidence in plain form tied to its real signal so later steps do not mistake fluency for knowledge.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large language models must be taught to know what they don't know
finding: Prompting alone is not enough for calibration. Finetuning on about 1,000 graded examples with LoRA gives better ECE and AUROC than prompting baselines. Models can estimate the uncertainty of other models too. A user study shows the estimates help people use the LLM.
numbers: About 1,000 labeled examples nearly as useful as 20,000. Prompted ECE does not improve as the base model improves. AUROC improves slightly, but even the best prompted model lags the worst finetuned one (LLaMA-2 7B).
quote: prompting on its own is insufficient to achieve good calibration
limits: Needs labeled correctness data and open weights for LoRA. Measured on MMLU-style and open-ended QA.
agent_relevance: If any small gate is trained, a thousand graded S0 outcomes may be enough. Without training, treat prompted gates as weak.

source: Binder et al. (2024) Looking inward: language models can learn about themselves by introspection
finding: Models finetuned to predict properties of their own behaviour beat a second model trained on the first model's behaviour. This is evidence of privileged self-access on simple tasks, and it fails on complex or out-of-distribution tasks.
numbers: Stated M1 over M2 advantage +17% for GPT-4o (Sec 3.2). GPT-4 self-prediction 49.6% vs cross-prediction plateau 36.2% at 20,000 samples; Llama 70b self 48.5%, cross by GPT-4o plateaus at 35.2%. GPT-3.5 shows only a +0.8% advantage (p=0.002).
limits: About behavioural properties, not facts. Fails on harder tasks.
agent_relevance: Self-knowledge exists but is narrow. S0 should be calibrated per task family and not assumed general.

source: Ji-An et al. (2025) Language models are capable of metacognitive monitoring and control of their internal activations
finding: Neurofeedback-style paradigm using in-context examples. Models can report and control some activation directions. Ability grows with the number of in-context examples, with how interpretable the direction is, and with the variance it explains. Only a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space' is monitorable.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; per-model numbers not recorded.
limits: Only a small subset of neural activity is monitorable. Safety angle: models might hide internal states.
agent_relevance: Limits what any self-report can see: the agent's monitor covers a thin slice of its own state.
